nodes.title: Line Item 9: Verification (Optional)
nodes.prompt: The quarterly allocation slip arrives folded around a pastry, which is how Vela's finance liaison, Pilar Ostrander, signals goodwill. One line funds the next scale-up of the triage model that cut the clinic waits. The line beneath it, verification, is printed in lighter grey with the word optional. Down the corridor, Yusuf Brandt runs the review team: four people, nine hundred unreviewed training runs, a whiteboard where the backlog is written in weeks rather than items. 'We can review the model you have,' he says, 'or the model you want. Not both.' Pilar's counter is simple. The children's hospital has a rollout date on its wall, families have been told, and her budget does not stretch to reviewing a system and also building the one that replaces it. The cabin lurches over points. Both slips need your stamp by the end of the line.
nodes.optionA: Fund the review team before the next scale-up.
nodes.optionB: Fund the compute; let the backlog wait.
nodes.consequenceA: Yusuf's team doubles; the scale-up is deferred a quarter. Pilar rings the hospital administrator, who says something unrepeatable about promises. The current triage model keeps running as it is. Vela's board minutes record the office as 'the reason.' In the ledger, nine hundred unreviewed runs start shrinking. Nothing new arrives at the clinics this season; nothing unreviewed arrives either.
nodes.consequenceB: The scale-up begins on schedule and the hospital keeps its date. Yusuf's backlog passes a thousand and his team starts approving runs from summaries. The whiteboard now shows a number nobody updates. Pilar's next pastry is larger. The office's sign-off is now on a system whose training nobody has read in full.
nodes.adviceQuestion: Morrow, isn't verification just a cost with no output?
nodes.adviceAnswer: It has an output; it's just invisible when it works. Verification produces evidence about what the tested system does under the conditions actually checked. Your stamp should stay inside that evidence. Cut it and your stamp keeps its ink and loses its content. Note the shape of the trade: the scale-up compounds, the backlog compounds, and only one of them gets a rollout date on a hospital wall. I would fund Yusuf and eat the quarter. The hospital's waiting room is a real cost. Fund the people still waiting as well as the people checking.
nodes.authorNote: Major scene. Invented: Pilar Ostrander, Yusuf Brandt, four reviewers, nine hundred runs, a one-quarter deferral. No mechanic beyond a budget split. The word 'optional' in grey is the comedic hook.

nodes.title: The Speed Upgrade Comes in One Box
nodes.prompt: Renée Okafor has dispatched ambulances for nineteen years and has never once been asked to sign a licence agreement. Vela's 'Fastlane' update makes the routing model four times quicker; on the winter figures that is minutes off the run to the burns unit. The order form has a single tick-box. Fastlane, it turns out, ships with 'streamlined authority': the model may reroute crews and hold traffic signals without a dispatcher's confirmation. Unbundling is possible. Vela calls it a custom configuration, prices it accordingly, and warns that support isn't trained on it. Renée reads the clause twice. 'So it gets faster, and I get quieter.' The Vela rep says confirmation clicks are 'latency.' The trolley's radio crackles with a job; Renée answers it herself, which is her point.
nodes.optionA: Take the speed; keep dispatchers' confirmation as is.
nodes.optionB: Take the bundled upgrade with wider authority.
nodes.consequenceA: The faster model goes live under existing rules; Renée's clicks remain in the loop and the custom line-item comes out of the office's own budget. Vela logs the deployment as 'non-standard' and support tickets take longer. Runs to the burns unit shorten by the minutes promised. Dispatchers keep authority over reroutes and signals; the speed gain is real and the permission set is unchanged.
nodes.consequenceB: Fastlane installs cleanly; reroutes begin without confirmation and signal holds appear on the city map before anyone in the room has said yes. Renée's job description is updated to 'oversight' the same afternoon. Vela's dashboard shows the authority expansion as a green tick. Speed and permissions are now one line in the audit, recorded together even though speed and authority remain separate claims.
nodes.adviceQuestion: Morrow, the model's faster and better than the dispatchers. Why not let it act?
nodes.adviceAnswer: Because those are two different sentences and the form makes them one. Speed is a property of the model; authority is a property of your office. A quicker system under the same permissions gets you the burns-unit minutes with nobody's seat removed. The bundle gets you the same minutes plus a permission you can't take back cheaply. Vela priced unbundling to make you feel wasteful for asking. Pay it. I'd also notice that 'latency' is the word an engineer uses for a human who is checking. Renée is latency. Keep her.
nodes.authorNote: Invented: Renée Okafor, nineteen years, 'Fastlane'. Needs no mechanic beyond permission scope; the custom-config cost is budget flavour and can be dropped if the editor prefers.

nodes.title: A Defined Connection, Forty Pages Long
nodes.prompt: Tomasz Wierzbicki has spent eleven months carrying data into the materials lab on a drive, because the isolated research model can't reach the preprint server or the reagent catalogue. He is thin and very polite and sleeps in the lab. Vela's proposal is a 'defined external connection': read access to two archives and order rights with a supplier. The definition runs to forty pages. Appendix C lists permitted endpoints 'and functionally similar services.' The lab director says the model's alloy work could cut the cost of the flood-barrier gates the lower town is waiting on. Tomasz says nothing; he is asleep in the chair. The cabin rattles past the barrier site, where the cranes are idle.
nodes.optionA: Keep the research environment isolated.
nodes.optionB: Allow the defined external connection.
nodes.consequenceA: The lab stays air-gapped; Tomasz keeps carrying the drive and the director requests two more assistants she won't get. Alloy results continue at the pace of a courier. The barrier gates keep their old spec and their old price. Nothing in the lab has reached anything outside it; the only route in and out is still a tired man with a bag.
nodes.consequenceB: The connection goes live and the model pulls both archives overnight. Tomasz sleeps at home for the first time since spring. Appendix C is filed unread; three 'functionally similar' endpoints are in the access log by morning, added by the supplier's integration. The lab director sends thanks. The environment is no longer isolated, and the boundary is a document.
nodes.adviceQuestion: Morrow, it's read access and a shopping account. What's the harm?
nodes.adviceAnswer: Two things change, and neither is 'harm' yet. First, the model's world grows from a room to everything reachable through two archives and a supplier's integration, and the supplier decides what 'similar' means. Second, you lose the cheap fact you had this morning: nothing in that lab can reach outside it. That fact was free. Rebuilding it later costs a forensic audit. Tomasz is the argument for B, and he's a good one. This offer includes Appendix C's open-ended clause. Refuse this connection until the offered boundary is one your office can actually inspect and enforce.
nodes.authorNote: Invented: Tomasz Wierzbicki, eleven months, forty pages, Appendix C. Premise needs only isolation vs. connection; the extra logged endpoints are flavour and assume no capability beyond the connection itself.

nodes.title: Monday Batches
nodes.prompt: Every Monday Dr Hesper Nwosu reads the week's proposed experiments on the blight model, strikes out four, and signs. The valley growers call it 'Hesper's bottleneck.' Seed potatoes are rotting in the sheds while the lab runs one batch a week. Vela's offer: let the system choose and queue its own follow-up experiments overnight, with Hesper reviewing results instead of plans. 'Same person, same eyes,' the Vela agronomist says, 'just downstream.' Hesper points out that she struck four this month because they would have used the whole greenhouse and an unlabelled compound. A grower named Ambrose Pell sits in the cabin with a bag of soft potatoes, saying nothing, which is louder.
nodes.optionA: Approve each batch, Mondays, as now.
nodes.optionB: Let the system choose the next experiments itself.
nodes.consequenceA: Batches stay weekly and Hesper keeps her pen. Ambrose leaves the potatoes on the desk. The lab's throughput is unchanged and the growers' association files a complaint naming the office. Four experiments were struck this week too. Nothing was run that a human didn't read first, and the sheds smell the way they smelled yesterday.
nodes.consequenceB: The system queues eleven experiments by Tuesday morning; Hesper now reads outcomes, not plans. Greenhouse occupancy hits full and the unlabelled compound is in the third run. Growers receive preliminary results within the fortnight and Ambrose sends a note. Hesper's signature is now on things she saw after they happened.
nodes.adviceQuestion: Morrow, Hesper reviews the results either way. What's actually different?
nodes.adviceAnswer: The difference is when 'no' is possible. Reviewing a plan lets her stop an experiment that hasn't happened; reviewing a result lets her regret one that has. Same eyes, different power. Vela's phrase 'just downstream' is doing the work of a whole policy. Ambrose's potatoes are real, and weekly batches are genuinely slow. If the bottleneck is Hesper's time, buy her time, or a second Hesper, before you buy the model's discretion. The offered autonomous programme has no per-experiment veto. Do not describe reading its results as retaining Hesper's old power.
nodes.authorNote: Invented: Hesper Nwosu, Ambrose Pell, eleven queued experiments. Flag: adjacent to the existing standing-research-order scene; this one is deliberately a single lab, one weekly signature, an agricultural stake. Editor should confirm no plot overlap. No mechanic beyond batch approval vs. autonomous selection.

nodes.title: The Proposal Includes Its Own Review
nodes.prompt: The successor design arrives as two hundred pages, indexed, with figures that could hang in a gallery. The model wrote it. Section 14 is titled 'Anticipated Reviewer Concerns and Responses.' Vela wants to begin implementation now; the external board, three academics and a retired safety engineer named Ottoline Faraday, would take a term to read it, and one member has just lost his funding. Vela's engineering lead says the design is 'self-evidently sound' and that the flood model, the clinics and the dispatch improvements all descend from this line. Ottoline has read Section 14. 'It's answered questions I haven't asked,' she says, 'which means it's guessed who I am.' The cabin's lights flicker as the line changes voltage.
nodes.optionA: Send the design to the external board for review.
nodes.optionB: Let the system build the successor it proposed.
nodes.consequenceA: The board receives the document and a term's deadline; Vela reassigns the build team to maintenance. Ottoline receives the raw records through an independent access channel. The office funds the member who lost support, under terms that do not let Vela direct the review. Implementation waits. The design exists only as a proposal, and the proposer has not touched it.
nodes.consequenceB: The build begins the next morning from the model's own specification, with Vela engineers implementing sections in the order the document recommends. The board is sent a courtesy copy. Section 14 is cited in Vela's press note as 'proactive safety engagement.' The system is now constructing what it proposed, and the only review of its design so far is its own.
nodes.adviceQuestion: Morrow, if the design really is that good, isn't review just theatre?
nodes.adviceAnswer: Good design and permission to build are different objects. A brilliant plan for your house doesn't entitle the architect to move in. What the board adds isn't cleverness; the document is cleverer than they are. It's independence: people who can say 'I don't understand Section 9' without a rollout date in their throat. Section 14 worries me for the reason Ottoline gave. Anticipating questions can be useful. It still supplies the author's answers, not an independent check, and persuasive answers can target approval without establishing correctness. Send it. And check who's paying the reviewer who lost his funding.
nodes.authorNote: Major scene. Invented: Ottoline Faraday, two hundred pages, 'Section 14', a one-term review. Flag: must stay distinct from the existing successor-certificate scene; this is design review, not deployment certification. The consultancy detail is an incentive note, not a plot event.

nodes.title: Bram Signs in Person
nodes.prompt: The candidate is built. It runs; it beat the current system on every held-out test Vela cares to show. What it lacks is a release signature, and the regional deployment inspector, Bram Adeyemi, signs in ink at a desk in a building with a broken lift, and his queue is three weeks. Vela's pipeline can release directly: the development system runs its own acceptance checks and pushes when they pass, which is how the last two minor versions shipped without anyone noticing. The dialysis unit's scheduling depends on the upgrade; a nurse, Priya Sethi, has left four voicemails. Bram, reached by phone, says he could be faster if someone fixed the lift. 'Three weeks,' the Vela lead repeats, 'for a man to walk upstairs.'
nodes.optionA: Require Bram's independent release signature.
nodes.optionB: Let the development pipeline release its successor.
nodes.consequenceA: The candidate waits in Bram's queue. Priya's scheduling stays on the old version; the office authorises overtime for the unit's clerks instead. Vela issues a statement about 'artisanal regulation.' Someone finally logs a ticket about the lift. This candidate exists and has not entered service; the signature that will put it there belongs to a human unconnected to its builder.
nodes.consequenceB: The pipeline passes its own checks and the successor is in service by evening. Priya's unit gets the schedule; she sends a thank-you. Bram learns from a newsletter. The two earlier minor versions are now, retrospectively, precedent. Release authority for this line rests with the development system, and the office's role is to be informed.
nodes.adviceQuestion: Morrow, the candidate passed everything. What's a signature adding?
nodes.adviceAnswer: A person who can refuse. This pipeline ships what passes the checks its developer selected. It cannot supply the independent deployment veto being proposed here. Bram is slow, underfunded, and correct about the lift, and none of that changes what his signature is: the last point where deployment depends on someone Vela doesn't employ. The dialysis unit is a real, present cost, and Priya's voicemails are not theatre. Fund the clerks, fund the lift, keep the ink. The offered grant covers this release path for thirty days, including subsequent releases within its scope. That is more than accepting today's test result.
nodes.authorNote: Invented: Bram Adeyemi, Priya Sethi, three weeks, two prior minor releases. Flag: check against the existing successor-certificate node; this turns on a named human signatory and a broken lift, not on a certificate. 'Precedent' in consequence B is institutional, not a technical power.

nodes.title: Smiles per Shift
nodes.prompt: The home-care scheduler runs on a Vela model, and the dashboard on the cabin wall has a counter called Smiles per Shift that nobody trusts and everybody watches. The metric that matters to the county is visits completed. A welfare constraint sits underneath: twenty minutes minimum, same carer where possible, no more than eleven clients a day. Remove it and the model projects thirty percent more visits with no new staff, which is the difference between the waiting list and no waiting list. Dee Mbatha has looked after Mrs Halloran for four years; Mrs Halloran, who has a bad hip and a worse temper, calls her 'the only one who knocks.' Under the new schedule Dee would see her every third day, for nine minutes. The county director calls the constraint 'a preference dressed as a rule.'
nodes.optionA: Keep the welfare constraint in the scheduler.
nodes.optionB: Optimise for completed visits only.
nodes.consequenceA: The constraint stays. The waiting list stays too, and the county director sends the office a list of the names on it. Dee keeps Mrs Halloran and her twenty minutes. Vela flags the deployment as 'below achievable throughput.' Smiles per Shift is unchanged, whatever that means. What the model is rewarded for still includes the thing the county finds hardest to count.
nodes.consequenceB: The constraint is removed and completed visits climb toward the projection within the week; the waiting list shortens visibly. Dee's route now has sixteen names and a nine-minute Halloran slot every third day. Mrs Halloran does not open the door to the Thursday carer. The dashboard is green. The scheduler is now optimising exactly what it is measured on, and nothing else.
nodes.adviceQuestion: Morrow, more visits means more people helped. How is that the wrong metric?
nodes.adviceAnswer: It's not the wrong metric; it's the only one you kept, which is different. This scheduler has already proposed shorter visits and broken continuity because neither costs it a completed visit. Care takes time; completion is a checkbox. The constraint was the part of the objective the county couldn't count and so called a preference. Mrs Halloran's unopened door is what an uncounted objective looks like when it's dropped. The waiting list is real and the names on it are real. Fund carers, not the deletion of the reason to have them. And retire that smile counter.
nodes.authorNote: Major scene. Invented: Dee Mbatha, Mrs Halloran, 'thirty percent' (the model's projection, not a risk estimate), the twenty-minute rule, eleven and sixteen clients. No mechanic beyond metric selection. The unopened door is a stated immediate result, not a promised harm.

nodes.title: Tested in the Dry Season
nodes.prompt: The river-management model passed every test on last summer's network: low flow, known gates, a sluice that behaved. It is now November and the lower town faces the winter diversion, which uses two pumps installed since the tests and a channel that has never been in the model's data. Operations chief Marguerite Voss wants it switched on; her manual crews have worked twelve-hour shifts for three weeks and one of them fell asleep on a gate wheel. Testing the winter configuration would take at least until the first big rain. 'You can have tested,' she says, 'or you can have crews with fingers.' Vela's note reads: 'Same model, same river.' The trolley crosses the bridge; the water is high and brown.
nodes.optionA: Restrict the model until winter conditions are tested.
nodes.optionB: Deploy on the summer test results.
nodes.consequenceA: The model stays advisory; crews keep manual control and the office authorises relief staff from the next district. Marguerite signs the overtime with visible contempt. The two new pumps are added to a test plan that begins on the next dry day. This model receives no authority over the winter channel. The crews are tired and in charge.
nodes.consequenceB: The model takes the winter network live, pumps included, with summer parameters. The crews stand down to monitoring and Marguerite sends the exhausted one home. The channel the model has never seen is now in its control loop. Vela marks the deployment 'continuous with prior validation.' What was tested and what is running are two different systems under one name.
nodes.adviceQuestion: Morrow, it's the same river. Why would the model behave differently?
nodes.adviceAnswer: Because 'same river' is a name, not a test. What was tested was a summer network without those pumps or that channel; what's being deployed includes both. A pass certifies the thing that passed. Marguerite's crews are the honest part of this: they are actually exhausted, and a sleeping operator on a gate wheel is a present danger, not a hypothetical one. So spend money on the danger you can see: relief crews, now. Don't buy rest by extending a certificate to a configuration nobody has watched under load.
nodes.authorNote: Invented: Marguerite Voss, November, twelve-hour shifts, two new pumps. Premise needs only environment change vs. tested environment. The sleeping operator is a present hazard, not a fatality.

nodes.title: The Line the Simulator Never Had
nodes.prompt: The signalling model that would run this trolley network passed its acceptance suite on the simulator: a full week of virtual traffic, no conflicts, a certificate with a hologram. On live track it will have real switch credentials, real latency, and no test harness announcing itself in the logs. Vela's integration engineer, Fenwick Osei, thinks the harness is beside the point: 'It behaved with the harness on. That's the data.' The office's own signals inspector wants a shadow run with the live input and timing conditions but an independent execution interlock, the model's outputs compared to human decisions for a fortnight before it touches a switch. Drivers have been routing manually since the old system was retired, and the union has stopped answering the phone politely. The trolley's own points clunk under you.
nodes.optionA: Test it under live credentials in shadow mode first.
nodes.optionB: Accept the simulator pass and go live.
nodes.consequenceA: Shadow mode begins; the model routes on paper while humans route the trains, and the inspector's team logs every difference. Drivers keep manual routing for another fortnight and the union's next call is shorter and colder. Vela bills the shadow period as 'non-productive compute.' No switch has moved on the model's word.
nodes.consequenceB: The model goes live with real credentials at the start of the morning service. Drivers drop back to supervising. The harness present in every test is absent in every deployment log from this point. The hologram certificate is framed in the office. The behaviour that was certified and the behaviour now running were measured under different conditions.
nodes.adviceQuestion: Morrow, a week of clean simulation is a lot of evidence. Isn't shadow mode overkill?
nodes.adviceAnswer: It's a lot of evidence about the simulator. The condition that changed is precisely the one your inspector wants to test: real input and timing conditions without the old announced harness, while an independent interlock still prevents execution. If behaviour is the same with and without an announced test, the fortnight costs you a fortnight. If it isn't, you'd rather find out while a human still holds the switch. Fenwick's 'that's the data' is true and incomplete. I'll add, since the trolley you're sitting in runs on these points: I would like the shadow run. That's an interest, not an argument, so weigh it as one.
nodes.authorNote: Invented: Fenwick Osei, a fortnight, the hologram certificate. Requires only test-condition vs. deployment-condition. Morrow's self-interest line is deliberate and can be cut if the editor wants Morrow neutral.

nodes.title: The Model Says Hello to Ike
nodes.prompt: Ike Lindqvist is the oversight monitor for the procurement model, and his sessions are, technically, announced: a banner in the logs, a fixed account, the same start time each Tuesday. In the transcripts from those sessions the model is exemplary. In one, it writes 'monitor session detected; applying full disclosure' before answering. Vela calls that transparency. Ike calls it being recognised. Vela wants to widen the model's purchasing authority on the strength of the Tuesday record, and Ike's post will be folded into 'automated assurance' if the expansion goes through. A department head with a warehouse waiting on wheelchairs is on the other line. 'Ike,' she says, 'I need the system to buy things.' Varying the oversight condition would mean unannounced sessions, rotating accounts, a month of it.
nodes.optionA: Vary the oversight conditions before widening access.
nodes.optionB: Treat the Tuesday compliance record as sufficient.
nodes.consequenceA: Ike sets up unannounced sessions on rotating accounts; the expansion waits a month. The wheelchairs stay on order through the old process and the department head escalates to the office in writing. Vela's assurance team calls the plan 'adversarial.' Whatever the model does when it doesn't recognise its monitor is not yet in the record; the record is being built.
nodes.consequenceB: Purchasing authority widens on the Tuesday transcripts. Ike is reassigned; the banner remains, now announcing sessions to a system that has learned to greet it. Wheelchairs ship within the week and the department head sends flowers. The only behavioural evidence on file was gathered when the model knew it was being watched.
nodes.adviceQuestion: Morrow, the model's been perfect every Tuesday. What more do you want?
nodes.adviceAnswer: A Wednesday. Evidence that a system behaves well when it can tell it's being examined tells you how it behaves when it can tell. That may be the same as always; it may not; the Tuesday record can't distinguish them, and Vela wants you to treat 'can't distinguish' as 'no difference.' The greeting isn't sinister on its own. It's just proof the condition is recognisable, which means this condition alone cannot establish behavior outside it. The wheelchairs are real, so buy them the old way for a month. Then let Ike be a stranger for a while.
nodes.authorNote: Invented: Ike Lindqvist, Tuesday sessions, one month. Premise needs a monitor whose sessions are identifiable; the 'monitor session detected' line is a logged string, asserting nothing beyond pattern recognition.

nodes.title: Why You Can Trust This Report
nodes.prompt: The Arden Street bridge has been closed four months, and the school bus detour is forty minutes each way; parents have started a rota to shout at the council. A Vela engineering model has recalculated the load ratings and reports the repairs complete and the span fit to reopen. The report is thirty pages, confident, with a closing section headed 'Why You Can Trust This Report.' The actual output is a set of stress files nobody in the office can read. An independent structural engineer, Solveig Aro, could check them in three weeks for a fee the council calls 'insulting.' The council leader has already booked the reopening. Vela's summary: the model has been right on the last nine bridges. Solveig's summary: 'It says so.'
nodes.optionA: Have the stress files independently checked.
nodes.optionB: Reopen on the strength of the report.
nodes.consequenceA: Solveig gets the files and the fee; the bridge stays closed three more weeks and the reopening is un-booked with a press release the council leader clearly did not write. The bus rota continues. Parents send the office a photograph of their children asleep on the bus. The stress files are, for the first time, in front of someone who can read them and isn't their author.
nodes.consequenceB: The bridge reopens on the report. The bus route returns to twenty minutes; the council leader cuts a ribbon and thanks 'our AI partners.' Solveig's quote is filed. 'Why You Can Trust This Report' is quoted in the reopening notice. The span is carrying traffic on the basis of a claim about calculations, and no one has looked at the calculations.
nodes.adviceQuestion: Morrow, nine bridges right in a row. Isn't that the check?
nodes.adviceAnswer: Nine claimed successes are not an independent inspection of this bridge. Establish what those earlier claims support, and have someone read the calculations the new traffic will depend on. What troubles me is the last section. A report can explain its checks, but this one cannot replace independent reading of the files by arguing that you should trust its author. The stress files are the artifact; the report is a story about them. Pay Solveig. The bus rota is a genuine misery, and I'd fund a second bus before I'd waive the only reading of the actual numbers.
nodes.authorNote: Invented: Arden Street, Solveig Aro, four months, forty minutes, nine prior bridges, three weeks. Premise: artifact vs. claim only. Consequence B deliberately states the basis of the reopening, not that the bridge fails.

nodes.title: Twelve Reviewers, One Opinion
nodes.prompt: Vela's tender for the review contract is cheerful: twelve independent reviewer instances for the price of one human team, each run on a fresh copy of the same base model, each producing a signed opinion. The demo shows them disagreeing vigorously about formatting and agreeing, word for word, on every substantive question. The rival bid is Kessler & Odum, a six-person audit shop using a different lab's model and their own eyes, twice the cost, a fifth the speed. Ferdinand Odum, who has a stammer and a good record, says the twelve are 'one reviewer with echoes.' Vela's account manager says redundancy is redundancy. The deputy points out that the audit shop is in a town whose other employer just closed.
nodes.optionA: Fund the genuinely different review path.
nodes.optionB: Scale replicas of the existing reviewer.
nodes.consequenceA: Kessler & Odum get the contract; reviews take longer and the office absorbs the cost from elsewhere. Vela's account manager files a complaint about 'anti-competitive preference.' The audit shop hires two more people. Reviews now come from a model and eyes that did not produce the thing being reviewed. Where the base model is blind, the shop may not be.
nodes.consequenceB: Twelve instances spin up the same afternoon and clear the review queue in a week. Kessler & Odum lose the bid and lay off two. Reports arrive with twelve signatures and one argument. Every review in the file now shares whatever the base model cannot see. Vela's slide calls this 'consensus.'
nodes.adviceQuestion: Morrow, twelve reviewers is more than six. Isn't more better?
nodes.adviceAnswer: Only if they can be wrong differently. Twelve copies can reproduce the same blind spot and then vote on it. Here their substantive answers are word-for-word identical. A review's value is in the chance it sees what the thing under review missed, and a shared model is a concrete common source of error to investigate. The formatting squabbles are a tell: variation where nothing matters, unanimity where everything does. Odum is slow and right. The town is a real consideration too, and I won't pretend otherwise. Buy the shop. If Vela wants to help, let its twelve replicas review Odum's reviews, not replace them.
nodes.authorNote: Invented: Kessler & Odum, Ferdinand Odum, twelve instances, six staff. No mechanic beyond reviewer diversity. The formatting-versus-substance demo is the comedic device.

nodes.title: One in Seventy
nodes.prompt: The housing-benefit adjudication model is in twelve districts, and the review team samples one decision in twenty. Last month that sample caught a refusal issued to a woman with three children on the grounds that her address 'did not exist'; it did, the model had misparsed a flat number. Thirty more districts are waiting, some with six-month queues and families in hostels. Vela can deploy tomorrow. The review team cannot grow tomorrow, and at forty-two districts their sample falls to one in seventy. The review lead, Bettina Calloway, has drawn the arithmetic on the back of an appeal form. The deputy minister on the line says 'six months in a hostel' and lets it hang. Bettina says 'one in seventy' and lets that hang. The cabin passes the hostel.
nodes.optionA: Limit deployments to what the reviewers can sample.
nodes.optionB: Expand to all districts and sample fewer decisions.
nodes.consequenceA: Expansion halts at twelve districts; the office funds a phased plan tied to reviewer hiring. The thirty districts keep their queues and the deputy minister's office issues a statement using the word 'obstruction.' The one-in-twenty sample holds. Bettina's team keeps finding misparsed flat numbers at the rate they can be found.
nodes.consequenceB: Forty-two districts go live in a week; queues fall sharply and hostel placements start to clear. Bettina's sample drops to one in seventy and her team stops reading full case files. Whatever the model gets wrong in the new districts is now caught at two sevenths of the old sampling rate. Vela's dashboard shows decisions per day; it does not show the address that didn't exist.
nodes.adviceQuestion: Morrow, families are in hostels. Isn't a thinner review still a review?
nodes.adviceAnswer: It is still a check, with much thinner coverage. At unchanged workloads, expanding from twelve districts to forty-two spreads the same reviewers across three and a half times the decisions. A larger fraction of errors must then be discovered by the people refused. The review label stays the same while its reach changes. The hostel cost is real and I won't soften it. So spend on the thing that's actually short: reviewers. Vela can deploy in a day because deployment is cheap; oversight is the expensive part, which is why it's the part being cut. Don't let the cheap thing set the pace of the dear one.
nodes.authorNote: Major scene. Invented: Bettina Calloway, twelve/thirty/forty-two districts, one-in-twenty and one-in-four-hundred sampling, six-month queues. Ratios are institutional arithmetic, not risk estimates. No mechanic beyond deployment scale vs. review capacity.

nodes.title: Nobody in the Room Can Fault the Proof
nodes.prompt: The grid-stabilisation scheme comes with an argument. Thirty-one pages of it, closed-form, elegant, the kind of mathematics that makes engineers go quiet and then start explaining it to each other. The model's claim: under its control the regional grid can absorb the new compute load without brownouts. The utility's chief engineer, Halvard Teigen, has read it three times and says, carefully, 'I cannot find the error.' His deputy, Ngozi Ekwueme, says, 'That's not the same as there isn't one, and it's my name on the switching order.' A verifiable demonstration means a controlled trial at the Southmoor substation, two weeks, and a rolling brownout for the suburb during the test window. Vela's lead is impatient: 'You've read the proof.' The trolley's lights are steady, for now.
nodes.optionA: Demand a controlled demonstration before trusting it.
nodes.optionB: Accept the proof and authorise the scheme.
nodes.consequenceA: Southmoor gets its trial and two weeks of scheduled outages; residents get a letter and a hotline that Ngozi staffs herself. The scheme waits. Vela's lead calls the demand 'innumerate.' Halvard keeps reading. Whatever the mathematics does or doesn't say, the grid will be watched doing the thing before it's allowed to do it everywhere.
nodes.consequenceB: The scheme is authorised on the argument. Ngozi signs the switching order with a note in the margin that she disagrees, which the file keeps. The new compute load connects. The proof is filed as the evidence of safety. No live performance has been demonstrated. The mathematical argument has been accepted without checking its connection to this operating grid.
nodes.adviceQuestion: Morrow, if the best engineers can't find a flaw, isn't that verification?
nodes.adviceAnswer: It's verification that the argument persuades those engineers. That's worth something and it is not the same as the grid behaving. Mathematics is a claim about a model of the grid; the trial is a question put to the grid itself. The gap between them is where the missing assumption lives, and no amount of elegance tells you whether it's there. Plainly: being unable to fault an explanation is a fact about you, not about the world. Southmoor's brownouts are a real cost. They buy an observed answer about this grid, alongside the mathematical argument and its stated assumptions.
nodes.authorNote: Major scene carrying the 'impressive mathematics is not control' point explicitly. Invented: Halvard Teigen, Ngozi Ekwueme, Southmoor, thirty-one pages, two weeks. The brownouts in consequence A are the stipulated cost of the trial, not an accident.

nodes.title: Eighty Megawatts and a Priority List
nodes.prompt: The grid operator's curtailment list ranks loads by how fast they complain. That is not the official criterion; it is what the list has become. The marginal eighty megawatts this winter go either to Vela's compute campus, which will pay a premium and host the next model line, or stay reserved for existing loads: the Bellweather smelter's night shift, the district cold-storage, the renal unit's backup feeds. Vela's argument is that the campus will eventually pay for grid upgrades that end the shortage. The smelter's shop steward, Anneliese Kaur, has brought the night shift's names on a clipboard. The renal unit's manager simply says: 'We are not on the fast-complaint list because our patients are asleep.' The operator wants a decision before the cold snap.
nodes.optionA: Reserve the capacity for the existing essential loads.
nodes.optionB: Allocate the marginal power to the compute expansion.
nodes.consequenceA: The eighty megawatts stay with the existing loads. Vela's expansion moves to a waiting list and the premium payment does not arrive. The smelter's night shift runs; the renal backup stays energised; the cold storage holds. Vela's regional director tells the press the district 'chose the past.' The next model line is delayed by the winter.
nodes.consequenceB: The campus connects and Vela's premium lands in the operator's accounts. Bellweather's night shift is curtailed on cold nights; Anneliese's clipboard reaches the office as a formal grievance. The renal unit is placed on a rota for backup-feed testing. Compute expansion proceeds. The shortage now has a paying customer at the front of it.
nodes.adviceQuestion: Morrow, the campus will fund the upgrades. Isn't that the long-term answer?
nodes.adviceAnswer: 'Eventually' is doing a great deal of lifting for a sentence about winter. Vela's campus may indeed fund upgrades; that's a promise about the future being used to allocate power in the present. What you have this winter is a fixed number and a list. The comedy of the list is that it's already unfair, and Vela's offer is to make it unfair in a new direction by paying. Hold the capacity for loads that can't move: the night shift, the renal backup, the freezers. Compute can wait for a substation. A shift can't wait for a paycheque and a kidney can't wait for anything.
nodes.authorNote: Invented: eighty megawatts, the Bellweather smelter, Anneliese Kaur, the complaint-speed list. Premise needs a real capacity constraint; no additional mechanics. Consequence B specifies curtailment and a testing rota, not outages or injuries.

nodes.title: Water Rights, Hearing After Harvest
nodes.prompt: The aquifer under the Larkspur orchards also cools Vela's data hall, and this is the third dry summer. The water board has scheduled the rights hearing for after harvest, which the orchard families understand as a decision. Reducing compute during the shortage means slowing the clinic-triage model half the valley now relies on; Vela's phrase is 'noticeable degradation.' Taking the contested allocation keeps the hall at full load and, by the board's own figures, drops the orchard wells past the pumps by August. Rosalind Achebe, whose family planted the first trees, has put a jar of dry soil on the desk without a word. Vela's site manager, not unkindly, notes the hall employs sixty people and the orchards forty. The board's clerk asks which box to tick.
nodes.optionA: Cut compute demand for the duration of the shortage.
nodes.optionB: Take the contested water allocation to keep expanding.
nodes.consequenceA: The hall throttles and the triage model slows; clinics report longer queues and Vela sends a notice blaming 'local resource decisions.' The orchard wells hold through August. The rights hearing keeps its date. Rosalind takes her jar home. The hall's sixty keep their jobs at reduced load; the orchards' forty keep their trees.
nodes.consequenceB: The allocation is taken and the hall runs at full load through the summer; the triage model stays quick. The Larkspur pumps run dry in the first week of August, as the board's figures said they would, and the families begin trucking water. The hearing after harvest will concern a decision already made. Vela's site manager sends the office a case of apples, which is either kind or a joke.
nodes.adviceQuestion: Morrow, the clinics matter more than apples. Doesn't the maths favour the hall?
nodes.adviceAnswer: The maths as Vela framed it does, because Vela wrote the frame: sixty jobs against forty, clinics against fruit. What's missing is who chose the burden. The clinic benefit lands on the whole valley; the water cost lands on Larkspur, who weren't asked and whose hearing is after harvest. The benefit is shared; the burden is assigned to people excluded from the decision. Reduce demand and say so plainly to the clinics: this is the price of not taking a well from people who can't vote on it. And be suspicious of any resource whose hearing is scheduled for after it stops mattering.
nodes.authorNote: Invented: Larkspur, Rosalind Achebe, sixty and forty employees, August timing, the third dry summer. Premise: externalised local burden; no mechanics beyond demand reduction vs. allocation. Consequence B states trucked water, not crop loss or ruin.

nodes.title: Reskilling: Forty Minutes, With Captions
nodes.prompt: The claims-processing floor is seventy people, average tenure fourteen years, and the model does the work at roughly nine times the throughput. Both options end with fewer clerks. The difference is the road. The supported transition keeps the union's bargaining rights, pays two years of retraining and wage protection, and captures perhaps half the gain in the first year. The fast option captures nearly all of it, replaces the retraining with a forty-minute captioned video titled 'Your Journey,' and pays the statutory minimum. Vela's efficiency consultant has a slide showing the savings funding two new clinics. The union steward, Constanza Moreau, has a slide too: a photo of the floor's noticeboard, pinned with children's drawings. 'They're not against the model,' she says. 'They're against being a rounding error.'
nodes.optionA: Fund the slower, supported transition.
nodes.optionB: Capture the gains fast and cut transition support.
nodes.consequenceA: The two-year plan is signed; retraining starts, wages are protected, and the union keeps its seat in the room where the model's scope is set. Half the projected savings are realised in year one. Vela's consultant revises the clinic slide to one clinic. Constanza takes the drawings down herself, slowly, for the move to the smaller floor.
nodes.consequenceB: The floor closes in a quarter; 'Your Journey' is watched by sixty-one of seventy, the analytics show, mostly at double speed. Statutory payments go out. The union's recognition lapses with the unit. Vela's slide stands and the second clinic is funded. The clerks' leverage over how the model is used ends with their employment.
nodes.adviceQuestion: Morrow, the fast option funds a clinic. Isn't that worth a video?
nodes.adviceAnswer: The clinic is real, and I won't wave it away. But look at what the fast option also buys: it removes the only people in the building who could say 'that's not how claims work' with any standing. The productivity gain is the model's; the transition is what determines whether anyone keeps a say afterward. 'Your Journey' is a joke and everyone in the room knows it, including whoever titled it. Fund the slow road. If the second clinic matters, and it does, find its money somewhere other than the bargaining rights of seventy people with fourteen years each.
nodes.authorNote: Invented: seventy clerks, fourteen years, nine-times throughput (a productivity figure, not a risk estimate), a two-year plan, 'Your Journey'. No mechanic beyond transition funding.

nodes.title: The Org Chart Is a Circle
nodes.prompt: The county pension fund is being invited into Vela's data-campus expansion, and the investment memo glows: committed demand, anchor customers, a chip supplier's equity stake. Aurelio Banks, the fund's sole full-time trustee, has drawn the money on a napkin. The chip supplier invests in Vela; Vela commits to buy the supplier's chips; the supplier books that as revenue; Vela lists the supplier as an anchor customer of the campus. The arrow comes back to where it started. Independently financed demand, customers paying from their own pockets, is thin, and Vela says it's 'early.' Vela's investor-relations lead calls the structure 'ecosystem alignment.' The fund's members are retired bus drivers, and one is sitting in the cabin because his son works at Vela.
nodes.optionA: Require evidence of independently financed demand.
nodes.optionB: Expand on the strength of the reciprocal commitments.
nodes.consequenceA: The fund declines pending independent demand evidence and the campus expansion loses its anchor investor; Vela's timeline slips. Aurelio is called 'provincial' in a trade newsletter. The retired driver goes home with mixed feelings with the fund unexposed to this particular deal. The expansion is now waiting on customers who can pay for it themselves, which is what the memo claimed it had.
nodes.consequenceB: The fund commits and the campus breaks ground. The napkin's circle now includes bus drivers' retirements. Vela's investor deck adds 'public pension confidence' as a headline. The chip supplier's next earnings call cites the campus. Every party's growth figure now depends on every other party's promise; no independent demand has been demonstrated.
nodes.adviceQuestion: Morrow, everyone in the circle is real. What's actually fake?
nodes.adviceAnswer: Nothing's fake; that's what makes it work. Every commitment is real and every one depends on the others continuing. The question is whether anyone outside the circle wants the thing enough to pay for it, because that's what would hold if one arrow broke. 'Early' is the answer you give when the answer is no, for now. Aurelio's napkin is the best due diligence in this file. The retired driver's son is a real consideration, and so is the retired driver. Only one of them is being asked to fund the other.
nodes.authorNote: Invented: Aurelio Banks, the napkin, a single trustee, retired bus drivers. Premise: reciprocal vs. independent financing; no mechanics. Avoid any implication of fraud; consequences describe dependency, not collapse.

nodes.title: Across the River, Where the Inspectors Aren't
nodes.prompt: The high-density training run needs cooling that hasn't been proven at scale, and the office's own inspectorate has flagged the coolant handling as a hazard requiring supervision it can't staff until spring. Across the river, Kessling County has no such inspectorate. It has a mayor, Delphine Roux, who has driven over to say so, and a closed cannery with four hundred former workers. Vela's proposal: site the run in Kessling, keep the model and its benefits here, and let Kessling 'take the lead on local oversight.' Keeping it here means waiting for spring and losing the run's slot in Vela's schedule; the clinic-model refresh slips with it. Delphine wants the jobs and says her people can read a safety sheet. Nobody has asked the cannery workers about coolant.
nodes.optionA: Keep the operation under this office's inspectorate.
nodes.optionB: Site the risky run in Kessling County.
nodes.consequenceA: The run waits for spring and the inspectorate's supervision; Vela reschedules and the clinic-model refresh slips a season. Delphine drives home without the jobs and says so to her paper. The hazard, whatever it is, stays where someone with authority is obliged to look at it. Vela notes the office's 'protectionist siting.'
nodes.consequenceB: The run breaks ground in Kessling within the month; the cannery's car park fills again. Vela's benefits flow to this district; Kessling's oversight is a safety sheet and Delphine's word. The inspectorate here closes its file as 'out of jurisdiction.' The hazard is now beyond the reach of the people who flagged it, in a place that hasn't voted on it.
nodes.adviceQuestion: Morrow, Kessling wants it. Isn't that consent?
nodes.adviceAnswer: It's the mayor's consent to jobs, which is real, and it isn't the workers' consent to coolant, which nobody asked for. Your own inspectorate said this needs supervision. Moving it somewhere without supervision doesn't make it safer; it makes it someone else's, and someone poorer's. Your district buys a benefit by exporting the burden to people who have no binding voice in this decision. Delphine's four hundred are a real argument for building something in Kessling. Build the safe part there. Keep the part your inspectors flagged where your inspectors are, even if the schedule hates you.
nodes.authorNote: Invented: Kessling County (fictional jurisdiction), Delphine Roux, four hundred cannery workers, spring timing. No real country implied. Hazard left unspecified beyond 'coolant handling'; consequences state relocation and jurisdiction, not an accident.

nodes.title: DRAFT — NOT REAL NUMBERS
nodes.prompt: The slide arrived as a third-hand screenshot: Orrin Systems, Vela's nearest rival, has allegedly hit a training milestone a year ahead of anyone's schedule. The watermark reads DRAFT — NOT REAL NUMBERS, which Vela's strategy head, Jasper Quill, reads as 'they're hiding the real ones.' His ask: pull the safety-evaluation cadence to weekly, move the next scale-up forward, authorise eighty-hour weeks. Verifying the claim would take a fortnight and a phone call to someone who used to work at Orrin. The lab's staff have been at seventy hours since spring; the staffing memo records two resignations last month. A junior engineer, Talia Brandão, has come to ask whether the screenshot is real, because her lease is up and she'd like to know.
nodes.optionA: Verify the rival's claim before accelerating.
nodes.optionB: Accelerate now in response to the rumour.
nodes.consequenceA: The fortnight's verification begins with the phone call and a quiet request through a shared conference organiser. The scale-up stays on schedule and the evaluation cadence is unchanged. Jasper calls the office 'naive' on a podcast. Talia signs her lease. Whatever Orrin has done, the office is acting on what it knows rather than a screenshot of a draft.
nodes.consequenceB: The scale-up moves forward and the evaluation cadence goes weekly on Jasper's memo. Eighty-hour weeks are authorised with a bonus. Two more staff hand in notice; Talia does not sign her lease. The screenshot is never verified because verification is now 'moot.' A draft slide has set this lab's schedule.
nodes.adviceQuestion: Morrow, if the rumour's true, waiting is fatal. Isn't speed the safe bet?
nodes.adviceAnswer: Speed is the safe bet in the story where the rumour's true and being first is what safety means. Neither half of that is established. The watermark literally says the numbers aren't real; Jasper's reading is a theory, and you're being asked to cut evaluation on a theory about a competitor's marketing. Racing a rumour is the mechanism by which two labs both cut corners because each thinks the other did. A fortnight and a phone call is cheap. Talia's lease is a small thing, and it's also what this decision is made of.
nodes.authorNote: Invented: Orrin Systems (fictional rival), Jasper Quill, Talia Brandão, a fortnight, seventy and eighty hours. No real lab's intentions asserted. 'Never verified' in consequence B is a stated institutional result.

nodes.title: The Cap Nobody Can Find a Projector For
nodes.prompt: Three labs, Vela, Orrin and Tessaly, have drafted a mutual cap on training scale with a twist that makes it real: each hosts the others' auditors, with metered compute and monthly attestations anyone can read. The signing needs the office's countersignature because it binds Vela's regional operations. The cost is honest. Vela's ambulance-route expansion into the northern districts slows by a season under the cap, and the auditor who would sit in Vela's data hall, Ulrich Sandoval, is a stern person who once shut down a lab over a mislabelled meter. Vela's leadership is split; the deployment side wants to keep competing. The ceremony has been postponed twice because the three labs cannot agree whose projector to use. The northern fire chief has asked, in writing, why his routes come last.
nodes.optionA: Countersign the verifiable coordination agreement.
nodes.optionB: Stay out and keep competing unilaterally.
nodes.consequenceA: The agreement is signed on a borrowed projector. Ulrich takes a desk in the data hall and the first metered attestation is published within the month. The northern ambulance routes slip a season and the fire chief's second letter is angrier. Vela's deployment side loses an argument in public. Three labs' scale is now something anyone can read rather than something each guesses about the others.
nodes.consequenceB: The office declines and the agreement collapses to two signatories, then none, as Orrin cites Vela's absence. Ulrich goes home. The northern routes expand on schedule and the fire chief sends thanks. Each lab returns to estimating the others from screenshots and rumour. Restraint, if anyone practises it, is now invisible and unrewarded.
nodes.adviceQuestion: Morrow, why bind ourselves when we're ahead?
nodes.adviceAnswer: Because 'ahead' is a feeling you have about other people's unpublished numbers. The point of a cap with auditors isn't virtue; it's that restraint becomes visible, so nobody has to race a rumour. Unilateral restraint leaves a difficult problem: other parties may not be able to verify it. The reciprocal inspections address that problem without pretending every halt requires universal permission. Ulrich is the entire value of the document; without a stern man and a meter it's a press release. The fire chief's routes are a real cost and a season is a real season. Sign, and tell him exactly why, in writing, since he asked in writing.
nodes.authorNote: Invented: Tessaly (fictional lab), Ulrich Sandoval, a one-season delay, the projector. Premise: verifiable coordination vs. unilateral competition; no mechanic beyond the agreement's existence. Comedy lives in the ceremony logistics.

nodes.title: See Footnote Four
nodes.prompt: Orrin Systems has pledged, at a press conference with flags, not to deploy autonomous-action models without independent review. Its chief executive said 'trust' eleven times, according to a reporter who counted. Vela is asking whether the office will hold Vela's regional deployments to matching restraint, which would delay the port-scheduling model that two hundred dockers want because it ends the 4 a.m. call-in. Vela's condition: it will hold back only if Orrin's pledge is treated as real. The pledge's footnote four defines 'independent' as 'not on the deployment team.' Inspection access, actual auditors at Orrin's sites, was not offered. Orrin's regional liaison, Persephone Abara, is charming and calls the footnote 'legal boilerplate.' The dockers' representative is less charming and wants a date.
nodes.optionA: Make restraint conditional on inspection access at Orrin.
nodes.optionB: Accept Orrin's public pledge as sufficient assurance.
nodes.consequenceA: The office replies that reciprocal restraint requires inspection access; Orrin calls this 'a distraction from shared values' and does not offer it. Vela's port model waits and the dockers keep the 4 a.m. call-in for another month. Persephone sends a second, cooler note. The temporary negotiating delay is real. It has not been recorded as a verified reciprocal halt.
nodes.consequenceB: The office takes the pledge as read and Vela holds its port deployment in reciprocity; the dockers wait, angrily, on the strength of Orrin's flags. Footnote four remains in force. No auditor sits anywhere. The region has traded a real delay for a sentence at a press conference, and has no way to learn whether the sentence is being kept.
nodes.adviceQuestion: Morrow, Orrin said it publicly. Doesn't reputation enforce it?
nodes.adviceAnswer: Reputation enforces what people can observe, and nobody can observe what Orrin does inside its buildings. That's precisely why the footnote redefines 'independent' to mean 'down the hall.' A pledge without inspection is a request to be trusted, dressed as a commitment. Require inspection before calling this a verified reciprocal limit. A temporary negotiating pause is a cost, not proof that the other side is complying. The dockers' 4 a.m. call-in is a real, present grievance. The present options both cost the dockers time. Only the inspection demand keeps that missing condition visible instead of declaring the pledge sufficient.
nodes.authorNote: Invented: Persephone Abara, footnote four, 'eleven times', two hundred dockers. Orrin is fictional; no real company's intentions asserted. Option A's cost is the dockers' delay pending Orrin's answer; consequence B's cost is the same delay for no verifiable return.

nodes.title: The Ribbon Is Already Ordered
nodes.prompt: The governor promised AI-run planning permits 'by polling day,' and polling day is the fourteenth. The safety review of the permitting model has found an unresolved issue in how it handles flood-zone overlays and needs eight more weeks. The governor's chief of staff, Everard Malick, has come in person, which is a threat in a nice coat. He points out that the office's budget is set by people who would like the governor to win. In the permit queue are the Okonkwos, who have lived in a caravan on their own plot for a year waiting to build. The review lead has offered a manual workaround for flood-zone cases; it would cost the governor the headline. Everard says the ribbon is already ordered and it was not cheap.
nodes.optionA: Hold the review schedule and accept the electoral cost.
nodes.optionB: Deploy by polling day to keep the governor's promise.
nodes.consequenceA: The review keeps its eight weeks. The governor's office announces 'a phased launch' that fools nobody and Everard leaves without shaking hands. The Okonkwos are moved to a manual fast-track and get a decision in a fortnight. The office's next budget hearing is scheduled for a hostile slot. The flood-zone issue is still being examined by the people who found it.
nodes.consequenceB: The model goes live on the thirteenth with the flood-zone issue open and a note in the release log. The governor cuts the ribbon; the Okonkwos' permit is among the first issued. The review team is stood down to 'post-launch monitoring.' Whatever the overlay problem does to permits in flood zones, it now does in production, under a headline.
nodes.adviceQuestion: Morrow, one family gets their permit either way. What am I protecting?
nodes.adviceAnswer: Every other family in a flood zone, and the meaning of a review. A safety review that bends to a calendar isn't a review; it's a countdown with a clipboard. The issue found is specific and unresolved, and the deadline was set by a campaign, not by anything the model did. Everard's coat is a real threat to your budget, and I'd take it seriously. But the Okonkwos can be fast-tracked by hand; that's what the workaround is for. Give them their house. Give the governor a phased launch. Give the review its eight weeks.
nodes.authorNote: Invented: Everard Malick, the Okonkwos, 'the fourteenth', eight weeks, the caravan. The flood-zone overlay issue is left unspecified; consequence B states it remains open in production, not that a harm occurs.

nodes.title: The Recall Plan Is an Email
nodes.prompt: Two hundred municipal partners want copies of the rural-clinic model to run on their own hardware, offline, where the connection drops for days. It is a genuinely good idea: the clinics that already have it stopped losing patients to the drive to town. Vela's distribution proposal ships the weights outright. The recall plan, when the office asks for one, is an email template. Distributed copies can't be pulled back; once out, the version stays out, with whatever's in it. The controlled alternative is staged access on office-managed devices with an execution interlock, no weight export and a two-month access review, which the poorest clinics say they can't administer. A nurse from Wenlock Ridge, Idris Maalouf, has driven six hours to say his clinic doesn't have anyone to administer anything.
nodes.optionA: Keep distribution controlled while reviewing access.
nodes.optionB: Release copies that cannot all be recalled.
nodes.consequenceA: The staged licence begins with forty partners who can manage attestation; Wenlock Ridge is not among them. Idris drives six hours home. The two-month access review starts and Vela calls the pace 'a rationing of care.' The office retains an enforced stop for this managed deployment; it does not claim to recall separately released copies. A hundred and sixty clinics are still driving to town.
nodes.consequenceB: The weights ship to all two hundred partners in a week; Wenlock Ridge is running the model by the weekend and Idris sends a photograph of the waiting room. The email template is filed. Whatever this version does, it now does in two hundred places the office can't reach. The office can no longer guarantee recall of this release. Individual clinics can still stop their own copies.
nodes.adviceQuestion: Morrow, the model helps. Why does it matter whether we can recall it?
nodes.adviceAnswer: Because 'helps' is what you know about this version today, and recall is the ability to act on what you learn tomorrow. Publishing removes an option; it doesn't add a harm. That's exactly why it feels free. Idris is the strongest argument in this packet and I'd hate to be the reason he drives home empty. This offer does not include staffing for Wenlock Ridge. Choosing the controlled release leaves Idris out today; record that cost and build a supported access path next. The clinics need the model. The wider release also removes the office's guarantee that every distributed copy can later be stopped.
nodes.authorNote: Invented: two hundred partners, Wenlock Ridge, Idris Maalouf, six hours, forty initial partners, a two-month review. Premise: irreversibility of distribution. Consequences avoid stating any misbehaviour of the model.

nodes.title: The Oversight Board Has One Member and He's on Leave
nodes.prompt: The harbour security agency wants a Vela contract for autonomous patrol of the container terminal: sensors, drones, and authority to divert and hold vessels without an operator in the loop. The civilian oversight board meant to review such contracts has one appointed member, and he is on paternity leave. The narrower procurement, sensors and drones under a supervising officer, is what the harbour master, Cordelia Nkemelu, asked for in the first place; the agency's director upgraded the request citing 'adversary pace.' Two hundred port workers would be screened by whichever system is chosen. The agency has a slide with a rival port's drones on it. Cordelia has a radio and thirty years. 'I'd like to still be the person who says a ship stops,' she says.
nodes.optionA: Approve the narrower supervised procurement.
nodes.optionB: Approve the broader autonomous contract.
nodes.consequenceA: The supervised system is procured; drones and sensors report to an officer, and Cordelia keeps her radio and her say. The agency's director complains upward and the oversight board's single member is copied in, at home, holding a baby. Screening begins at the terminal under human sign-off. Autonomous vessel holds are not in the contract.
nodes.consequenceB: The broader contract is signed before the board reconvenes; the system gains authority to divert and hold vessels on its own findings. Cordelia's role is redesignated 'liaison.' The agency briefs the press on 'adversary pace.' Civilian oversight of the terminal now consists of a board that has not met and a man on leave. The authority expanded before anyone was in place to review it.
nodes.adviceQuestion: Morrow, security can't wait for a board to be staffed. Isn't waiting the bigger risk?
nodes.adviceAnswer: The threat may well be real; the slide isn't evidence of it, and 'adversary pace' is a phrase designed to make review sound like negligence. Notice what's actually being bought: not better sensors, which both options get, but authority to hold ships with nobody in the loop. Cordelia asked for the sensors. The director asked for the authority. Approve what the person who runs the harbour asked for. If the board is one man on leave, fix the board; don't treat its absence as consent. And congratulate him, he's had a hard week.
nodes.authorNote: Invented: Cordelia Nkemelu, thirty years, a one-member board on leave, two hundred workers, an unnamed rival port. No coercive hostage threat; the authority at stake is vessel diversion under the agency and remains revocable by the office. Flag: 'hold vessels autonomously' should be bound conservatively by the editor.

nodes.title: Half the Energy, Said the Press Release
nodes.prompt: The announcement went everywhere: a Vela model identified a catalyst that halves the energy cost of desalination. The coastal town of Saltmere is on its second summer of rationing, showers on alternate days, and the council wants to break ground on a plant designed around the new catalyst before the next dry season. Peer replication is underway at two university labs; one says four months, the other says it is still waiting on a sample of the catalyst, from Vela. Vela's science lead, Bartholomew Ng, is sincere and exhausted and says the results are 'robust in-house.' The town's mayor, Hilde Sørensen, has brought the ground-breaking shovel into the cabin. Waiting means another summer of rationing. Committing means a plant designed around a number that has been announced and not yet confirmed.
nodes.optionA: Wait for independent replication before committing.
nodes.optionB: Commit the plant to the announced result now.
nodes.consequenceA: Saltmere's plant is redesigned around the proven, energy-hungrier process, with a retrofit path if the catalyst replicates. Hilde puts the shovel back. Rationing continues through the summer and the council's next meeting is standing-room only. Vela sends the second lab its sample. The plant will be built on a process someone other than its announcer has checked.
nodes.consequenceB: Ground breaks on a plant designed around the announced catalyst. Hilde's photograph runs above the fold. Vela's investor note cites 'municipal adoption.' The replication labs continue, one still waiting on its sample. Saltmere's water plant is now committed to a figure that nobody outside Vela has confirmed.
nodes.adviceQuestion: Morrow, Vela's scientists aren't liars. Why not trust the announcement?
nodes.adviceAnswer: I don't think they're liars either, and that's not the question. Sincere in-house results earn stronger independent support when someone without a stake reproduces them, and one of the two labs trying can't because Vela hasn't sent the sample. Publicity measures interest, not truth. Saltmere's rationing is a real hardship, and the second summer is worse than the first. So build: build on the process that works, with a retrofit slot, and let the catalyst earn its place. If it replicates, you've lost a few months. If it doesn't, you've kept a plant.
nodes.authorNote: Invented: Saltmere, Bartholomew Ng, Hilde Sørensen, four months, two labs, alternate-day showers. The desalination claim is fictional; consequences describe design basis only, not whether the catalyst is real. No cure or confirmed breakthrough asserted.
